questions.question: animation-direction: alternate makes the animation:

options.text: Play forward then backward on alternate iterations

questions.explanation: With iteration-count > 1, alternate reverses direction each cycle — ideal for ping-pong/yo-yo effects.

questions.question: animation-play-state: paused is useful for:

options.text: Pausing/resuming via hover or JS without restarting

questions.explanation: Toggling play-state pauses/resumes in place — common for hover-to-pause or scroll-based control.

questions.question: step-end (steps) timing creates:

options.text: Discrete jumps with no interpolation (e.g. sprite frames)

questions.explanation: steps() divides the animation into equal intervals with no tweening between — perfect for sprite animation or tick effects.

questions.question: The will-change property:

options.text: Hints the browser to prepare for an upcoming change (e.g. transform) for smoother animation

questions.explanation: will-change (e.g. will-change: transform) lets the browser promote a layer ahead of time. Use sparingly — overuse wastes memory.

questions.question: Animating 'left'/'top' is generally worse than transform because:

options.text: It triggers layout (reflow) on every frame instead of cheap compositing

questions.explanation: Position changes cause reflow; transform/opacity run on the compositor. Animate transform: translate() instead of top/left.

questions.question: A keyframe at 50% with no 0%/100% still works because:

options.text: The browser uses the element's current computed value for the missing 0% and 100%

questions.explanation: Missing 0%/100% keyframes are synthesized from the element's existing styles, so partial keyframes interpolate from the base.

questions.question: To run two animations on one element:
questions.explanation: animation is a list; comma-separate multiple values to run several animations with independent timing.

questions.question: Best accessibility practice for non-essential animation is:

options.text: Wrap it in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to disable/reduce it

questions.explanation: Respecting reduced-motion prevents discomfort for vestibular-sensitive users — an essential a11y step.
